To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

early and correct diagnosis of childhood asthma is essential for early and adequate treatment and prevention of both under- and over-treatment, and that easily available data may facilitate this diagnosis.

the risk of adolescent asthma increased in children who had recurrent wheezing illness at age 4-6 years, and was higher in children with a family history of asthma or atopic dermatitis and/or a low social-economic background.

the combination of the frequency and the age of onset of the wheezing illness, respiratory and atopic symptoms at age 0 to 6 years and the sociodemographic parameters, may facilitate the diagnosis of asthma in young children.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the early detection of asthma and the prevention of under-and over-treatment.
the question whether the early and correct diagnosis of wheezing illnesses in children can be improved.
the question whether a combination of easily available data can help the general practitioner to make an early and accurate diagnosis of asthma in childhood.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

a child with recurrent wheezing illness at age 4-6 years with a positive family history of asthma, atopic dermatitis or sinusitis is more likely to have asthma than a child with recurrent or non-recurrent wheezers at age 0-6 years with no family history and no atopic dermatitis.
the risk for asthma increases with recurrent wheezing in the first 6 years of life, especially when this occurs in the first 3 years.
recurrent wheezing in the first 3 years of life is a risk factor for asthma, but that the absence of recurrent wheezing does not rule out asthma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the risk for asthma in children with recurrent wheezing illness increases with increasing age of onset of the wheezing illness and that this risk is further increased by the presence of atopic and respiratory morbidity.

a history of non-recurrent and recurrent wheezings in early childhood, in combination with a family history of asthma, atopic dermatitis, sinusitis and low socio-economic status, increases the risk for asthma in early childhood.
early and accurate diagnosis of asthma is essential for early and correct treatment of asthma and for prevention of under- or over-treatment of children with wheeziness.
